relations.note: Athirat is conventionally understood as El’s senior female partner and divine consort.
Athirat approaches El and persuades him to authorize Baal’s palace.
El asks Athirat to nominate one of her sons for Baal’s throne.
Baal sends costly gifts fashioned by Kothar-wa-Hasis to gain Athirat’s support.
Athirat intercedes with El and helps obtain authorization for Baal’s palace.
After Baal’s disappearance, Athirat proposes her son Athtar as his replacement.
Biblical texts juxtapose Baal worship with asherah objects but narrate no marriage or conversation.
Anat approaches Athirat for Baal and facilitates or joins her journey to El.
Modern and late comparisons sometimes fuse Anat with Asherah despite their Ugaritic distinction.
Kothar-wa-Hasis crafts the prestigious gifts Baal uses in his appeal to Athirat.
Athirat’s attendant prepares and accompanies her journey, serving as messenger, driver, or fisherman.
Athirat may participate in deliberations about Yamm’s kingship; her sea-related title remains disputed.
Athtar is named as Athirat’s son, though divine kinship may also indicate clan membership.
Athirat nominates Athtar for Baal’s throne, which he proves unable to occupy.
The seventy gods constitute Athirat’s offspring or divine clan, though the synthesis is partly reconstructive.
Athirat and Raḥmay appear together in a nursing formula for the gracious gods.

relations.myth: Birth and nursing of the gracious gods
relations.note: The voracious gracious gods receive milk from Athirat and Raḥmay.
In the Hittite-transmitted myth, Ašertu is explicitly the wife of Elkunirša.
After learning of Ašertu’s attempted seduction, Elkunirša orders or permits her humiliation or beating.
Ašertu attempts to seduce the Storm-god, who rejects and reports her approach.
Ishtar or Šauška intervenes or advises in the damaged conclusion; her precise role is uncertain.
Ašratum is paired with Amurru in Mesopotamian theology, but no narrative interaction survives.
relations.source: Old Babylonian god lists and cultic material

relations.note: Regional blessings associate Yahweh with his ʾšrth, possibly a consort, manifestation, or cult symbol.
Scholars compare Baalat Gebal or Dione with Athirat as Kronos-El’s wife; Philo never explicitly equates them.
Scholars sometimes identify Kronos-El’s wife Rhea with Asherah, but the proposed equation is disputed.
Later iconography and popular retellings merge Astarte with Asherah, although Ugaritic texts distinguish them.
Older scholarship equated Athirat with Qudšu, but the identification is now heavily disputed.
Asherah is sometimes equated with Atargatis, but continuity between them is a modern comparative proposal.
relations.source: De Dea Syria and modern studies

relations.note: Modern comparisons sometimes fuse Tanit with Asherah, without an early text establishing their identity.
